summary: Defines how SOAP messages, the XML-based messaging format used for remote procedure calls and notifications, are carried over BEEP, a framework for building application protocols. This binding describes how SOAP messages are transmitted across the network when BEEP is the underlying transport. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: SOAP is a way of writing messages in a standard format, and BEEP is a delivery truck. This memo says how to load the SOAP messages onto the BEEP truck so they arrive properly.

questions: how to send soap over beep
what is the beep profile for soap
what is the difference between soap.beep and soap.beeps
subtitle: How SOAP envelopes ride inside BEEP channels, with two URL schemes and a family of versioned profiles.

tldr.problem: SOAP defines an XML message format and message patterns, but it needs a binding that says how those messages are actually sent over a network. BEEP is a framework for application protocols that can serve as that carrier.
tldr.mechanism: A BEEP profile named http://iana.org/beep/soap/VERSION carries each SOAP envelope in a BEEP message. A short boot exchange picks the resource, and the standard BEEP MSG, RPY, ANS and NUL messages implement the SOAP exchange patterns.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4227 obsoletes RFC 3288, supports SOAP 1.2 as required and SOAP 1.1 as optional, and adds MTOM/XOP packaging. It has since been updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 4227 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2006. It obsoletes RFC 3288 and has been updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: What the Binding Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4227 specifies how SOAP envelopes are transmitted using a BEEP profile. An envelope is the top-level XML element that SOAP senders and receivers exchange. A SOAP binding describes how SOAP messages are transmitted in the network, and BEEP (the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol, defined in RFC 3080) supplies the transport machinery.

Conforming implementations MUST support SOAP version 1.2 and MAY support other versions, such as SOAP version 1.1. Unlike its predecessor RFC 3288, this memo does not mandate SOAP 1.1.
sections.eli5: SOAP is a way to write messages in a standard shape. This memo explains how to hand those messages to BEEP so they travel safely to the other computer.

sections.title: Profile Identification and the Boot Exchange
sections.content:
The BEEP profile for SOAP is identified in the BEEP profile element as http://iana.org/beep/soap/VERSION, where VERSION is the numeric SOAP version, for example http://iana.org/beep/soap/1.2. RFC 3288 used the plain http://iana.org/beep/soap for SOAP 1.1, so an implementation that chooses to support SOAP 1.1 should recognize both that URI and http://iana.org/beep/soap/1.1.

A channel is in one of two states. In boot, the peer that asked for the channel sends a bootmsg. If the other peer answers with a bootrpy the channel enters ready; if it answers with an error, nothing changes. In ready, either peer can start a SOAP message pattern by sending a MSG containing an envelope.

The boot message serves two purposes: resource identification (each channel gives access to one resource) and feature negotiation. Its resource attribute is analogous to the HTTP request path, and its optional features attribute lists feature tokens the sender would like to use. The reply may carry a subset of those tokens, and if it carries none, no features may be used. The serverName attribute of BEEP's start element plays the role of the HTTP Host header.
sections.eli5: Before sending any real mail, the two sides do a quick hello: one asks for a particular mailbox, and the other either says yes or says it does not have that one.

sections.title: How Envelopes Are Packaged
sections.content:
Envelopes are encoded as UTF-8 and SHOULD use the media type application/soap+xml. To stay compatible with RFC 3288, an implementation MAY use application/xml instead.

An implementation may also support the MTOM and XOP packaging techniques, which send binary parts such as an image next to the envelope in a MIME Multipart/Related package. If it does, it SHOULD support the MIME Multipart/Related XOP package format. Because BEEP provides an 8-bit-wide path, a transformative Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable should not be used.

Appendix A (informative) keeps the older SOAP with Attachments style, where the envelope is the root part of multipart/related content, as an option for compatibility with RFC 3288.
sections.eli5: The message goes in an envelope written in a standard way. If you also want to send a photo, you can tape it to the envelope in a package, without turning it into a different code first.

sections.title: Message Patterns and Errors
sections.content:
The profile maps SOAP patterns onto the BEEP exchange styles. A one-way message is a one-to-many exchange: the client sends a MSG with an envelope and the server immediately answers with a NUL, before it processes the envelope. A request-response is a one-to-one exchange: MSG with an envelope, answered by an RPY with an envelope. A request with N responses is a one-to-many exchange: MSG, then zero or more ANS messages each holding an envelope, then a NUL.

SOAP faults are not sent as BEEP ERR messages. Whatever SOAP response the server generates, faults included, comes back in the RPY (one-to-one) or in the ANS messages (one-to-many). An ERR is used only for problems with the BEEP message unrelated to the envelope, such as a badly formed MIME message or an unsupported content type.
sections.eli5: If you just drop off a letter, the clerk says 'got it' straight away. If you ask a question, the clerk writes back an answer. If something is wrong with the envelope itself, the clerk hands it back with a note, but a problem inside the letter is answered as part of the normal reply.

sections.title: Binding Conformance and Node Behavior
sections.content:
The binding is named by the same URI as the BEEP profile. The base URI for an envelope is the URI of the resource named in the bootmsg. An implementation MUST support the SOAP request-response message exchange pattern and MAY support the SOAP action feature.

The peer that starts an exchange may take the RequestingSOAPNode role and the other peer the RespondingSOAPNode role. The requesting node moves through Init, Requesting and Sending+Receiving to the terminal state Success, or to Fail if the first thing it receives back is a BEEP ERR. To avoid deadlock during streaming, the requesting node MUST be able to process incoming response information while the request is still being sent.
sections.eli5: The side that asks keeps track of where it is: just started, still talking, listening for the answer, and finally done or failed. It must be able to listen while it is still talking, so nobody gets stuck waiting.

sections.title: The soap.beep and soap.beeps URL Schemes
sections.content:
The memo defines two URL schemes, soap.beep and soap.beeps, which identify SOAP over BEEP over TCP. The path of the URL maps to the resource in the boot message and defaults to / if absent. For example, soap.beep://stockquoteserver.example.com/StockQuote corresponds to the boot exchange shown in the RFC.

Address resolution depends on the authority part. With a domain name and a port, the DNS is queried for A records and the port is used directly. With a domain name and no port, the DNS SRV algorithm is used with service soap-beep and protocol tcp (for example _soap-beep._tcp.stockquoteserver.example.com); if no SRV records are found, A records are used with the port IANA assigned. With an IP address, the DNS is not queried.

The soap.beeps scheme is identical except that the BEEP session must first be tuned for privacy, either by starting a transport security profile or a user authentication profile that supports transport security. After tuning, both peers issue a new greeting.
sections.eli5: A web-style address tells you which server and which mailbox to use. The version ending in 's' means 'lock the door first, then talk'.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Service provisioning is a policy matter, but at a minimum all implementations MUST provide these BEEP tuning profiles: http://iana.org/beep/SASL/DIGEST-MD5 for authentication, and http://iana.org/beep/TLS using the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher for confidentiality. For both together, the TLS profile is used with client-side certificates.

Implementations may also offer MIME-based security for message integrity and confidentiality, such as OpenPGP or S/MIME. BEEP-specific security issues are discussed in Section 9 of RFC 3080.
sections.eli5: The memo says every implementation must know at least one way to check who you are and one way to scramble the conversation so outsiders cannot read it.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3288
sections.content: RFC 4227 differs from RFC 3288 in one substantive way: a URL prefix is defined to support a family of BEEP profiles for different SOAP versions, and the IANA registrations were broadened to match. Support for W3C MTOM/XOP packaging was added, along with a section on the distributed state machine of the request-response pattern. A small number of typographical errors were corrected.
sections.eli5: The new edition lets one set of rules cover several versions of SOAP and adds a way to send attachments, while keeping the old way working.

messages.label: RPY (envelope)
messages.note: One-to-one: a single reply. SOAP faults also come back here.

messages.label: MSG (envelope)
messages.note: A second request, this time one-to-many.
